faqs.a: Roughly: below 1% is low, 1-3% is average, 3-6% is good, and above 6% is excellent. Smaller accounts typically engage better, so judge against similar-sized accounts in your niche.
faqs.q: What is a good engagement rate?

faqs.a: The most common standard uses followers as the denominator. Some analysts use reach or impressions instead, which gives lower numbers. For fair comparison, always check which denominator is being used.
faqs.q: Should I divide by followers or by reach?

faqs.a: Follower growth helps because the denominator grows, but not automatically: if new followers do not engage, your rate falls. Growing an engaged audience raises the rate; growing a passive one lowers it.
faqs.q: Does more followers mean higher engagement?

faqs.a: Because the audience is larger and more passive. A nano account can hit 8% while a million-follower account celebrates 2%. Brands know this, which is why smaller creators get such good deals.
faqs.q: Why do big accounts have lower rates?

faqs.a: Usually yes, but not always. Bots can inflate likes. Read the comments: real engagement has genuine conversation, while fake engagement shows generic one-word replies from odd accounts.
faqs.q: Does high engagement mean real influence?

faqs.a: Stories, reels, and polls for quick feedback, then this calculator for the numbers. Track the rate weekly, test one change at a time, and keep what moves the needle.

engagement-rate-calculator.formula:
Total interactions = Likes + Comments + Shares + Saves
Engagement rate % = (Total interactions / Followers) x 100
Example: (1,200 + 150 + 80 + 60) / 25,000 x 100 = 5.96%.

engagement-rate-calculator.workedExample:
Likes 1,200, comments 150, shares 80, saves 60, followers 25,000:
1. Total interactions = 1,200 + 150 + 80 + 60 = 1,490.
2. Engagement rate = (1,490 / 25,000) x 100 = 5.96%.
3. Per metric: likes 4.80%, comments 0.60%, shares 0.32%, saves 0.24%.
4. Verdict: 5.96% falls in 3-6%, so the rate is Good.
